balance.argument_a: The Smooth Curve is cheaper to compute, matches the real published table almost exactly at every age the firm has direct experience with (it is anchored to the real values at ages 90 and 99), has never triggered a regulatory objection on any other Highline filing, and never requires special-casing a boundary -- one formula covers every age from 0 to 120.
balance.argument_b: The Full Table is what the actual published mortality table says, including its own closing convention; it avoids materially under-reserving the exact cohort where the real table jumps, and it is defensible under audit because it uses the prescribed table as printed rather than a firm-built approximation of it.
balance.margin_basis: Blended dollars of reserve required per $1,000 of total face value, across Highline's full Horizon Series in-force block (Appendix D), computed once with the Smooth Curve formula (Appendix B) applied to every age and once with the Full Table (Appendix C) applied to every age including its age-100-and-over closure value.

computed_values.age_100_cohort_share_of_total_gap_pct_no: Share of the SUM OF ABSOLUTE per-age dollar differences ($9,354.42), not of the net portfolio gap ($1,089.26) — the net gap is smaller than any single age-100 term because other ages partially offset in the opposite direction. Corrected 2026-08-20 from an erroneous 95.7 found during packet build; independently reverified by hand from the Appendix B/C/D per-age tables.

modeling_assumptions.statement: The Smooth Curve's formula, C_A(x) = 1000 - 851.8963(0.973722)^(x-90), an exponential-approach-to-asymptote curve with asymptote fixed at $1,000, calibrated to pass exactly through the real published C_B(90) and C_B(99) values.
modeling_assumptions.why: No public source publishes a specific firm's own proprietary mortality-smoothing formula. The Kannisto model (S4) establishes that this general style of formula -- a smooth curve approaching a fixed asymptote -- is genuine, real, standard practice for old-age mortality. This case constructs one specific, worked, fully-shown example in that family rather than presenting a firm's confidential parameters as if they were public.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's central finding -- that the Full Table has a genuine boundary the Smooth Curve does not -- holds for any smooth, boundary-free formula in this family. Changing the calibration shifts the exact dollar figures without changing which method is continuous at age 100.

modeling_assumptions.statement: Highline's Horizon Series in-force block (Appendix D) uses contract counts by attained age equal to the real CDC survivorship (l_x) values from Appendix C's source table, scaled down by a factor of 200 and rounded to whole contracts.
modeling_assumptions.why: Highline is a fictional company; no real in-force block exists to cite. The relative shape of the age distribution is grounded in real national survivorship data rather than invented outright; only the absolute company scale (534 total contracts) is a stated scenario choice.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The portfolio-wide margin (D5) is sensitive to this scaling -- a block with proportionally more contracts exactly at the age-100-and-over boundary would produce a larger margin; fewer would produce a smaller one.

modeling_assumptions.statement: All worked numbers in this case use the CDC's Table 1 (2022) rather than the SOA 2012 IAM Basic Table's own values, even though the SOA table is the real industry standard for annuity valuation.
modeling_assumptions.why: The SOA table's specific qx digit values could not be independently verified through its interactive online lookup tool during research for this case (see RESEARCH_LOG.md). The CDC table is a direct government data-file download, independently checkable by anyone.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None on the dilemma itself -- this is a substitution of dataset, not a numeric assumption that could flip which method wins. Both tables share the real structural feature (a published table that stops at a top age and closes with a special convention) that the case is built around.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The Smooth Curve's coefficient k (MA1) is a good-faith calibration fit to the two real published anchor points at ages 90 and 99 (Appendix C); no firm publishes its own proprietary smoothing formula, so k is not independently sourced and a +/-50% flex (which breaks the fit to those real anchors) can flip which method looks cheaper in blended terms.

The Smooth Curve's decay-rate coefficient b (MA1) is a good-faith calibration fit to the same two real anchor points as k, for the same reason (no public source for a firm's proprietary formula); a +/-50% flex likewise breaks the anchor fit and can flip the blended-cost verdict.

The age-100-and-over cohort's contract count (MA2) is a stated scenario scaling of real CDC survivorship data for a fictional insurer; it is the single most sensitive dial per the case's own MA2 sensitivity note, and a -50% flex can flip which method looks cheaper in blended terms even though the underlying single-cohort discontinuity finding (D1-D4) is unaffected.

sensitivity_note: LOW (SPEC §6). This case's math is built entirely on aggregate, population-level mortality statistics -- the probability that a person of a given age dies within a year, drawn from a published national table -- never framed around any individual's death. Facilitators should keep classroom framing on the pricing decision (reserve adequacy, regulatory compliance) rather than personalizing the mortality figures. No further flag needed beyond this note.

cohort_bands.note: The 45-minute Socratic plan (FACILITATOR.md) runs as written, with two deep-conflict threads at 20:00-30:00 (cost-efficiency vs. regulatory-defensibility; aggregate-margin vs. per-cohort-adequacy).

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into a single pass. The twist still drops at 15:00, but only one deep-conflict thread runs (cost-efficiency vs. regulatory-defensibility); the per-cohort-adequacy thread is folded into the close-out discussion instead of run separately. Total runtime shortens proportionally.

There is no vote to take. Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a cold-call vote. The guide plays devil's advocate directly, arguing the other method's case rather than cold-calling other Heroes. The twist still lands, but 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why.'
